entries.e03c92d3e70b44623b8db837bb87a367a0b37b97: <div sID="gen9452" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="Job.10" sID="Job.10"/> <div eID="gen9452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9453" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9454" type="x-p"/> Job owns here that he was full of confusion (<reference osisRef="Job.10.15">ver. 15</reference>), and as he was so was his discourse: he knew not what to say, and perhaps sometimes scarcely knew what he said. In this chapter, I. He complains of the hardships he was under (<reference osisRef="Job.10.1-Job.10.7">ver. 1-7</reference>), and then comforts himself with this, that he was in the hand of the God that made him, and pleads that, <reference osisRef="Job.10.8-Job.10.13">ver. 8-13</reference>. II. He complains again of the severity of God's dealings with him (<reference osisRef="Job.10.14-Job.10.17">ver. 14-17</reference>), and then comforts himself with this, that death would put an end to his troubles, <reference osisRef="Job.10.18-Job.10.22">ver. 18-22</reference>.
entries.2c0228eeef48dd5ceef37aad3431765e41b062ef: <div eID="gen9454" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9453" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Job's Reply to Bildad. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9455" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> My soul is weary of my life; I will leave my complaint upon myself; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul. 2 I will say unto God, Do not condemn me; show me wherefore thou contendest with me. <hi type="super">3</hi> <hi type="italic">Is it</hi> good unto thee that thou shouldest oppress, that thou shouldest despise the work of thine hands, and shine upon the counsel of the wicked? <hi type="super">4</hi> Hast thou eyes of flesh? or seest thou as man seeth? 5 <hi type="italic">Are</hi> thy days as the days of man? <hi type="italic">are</hi> thy years as man's days, <hi type="super">6</hi> That thou enquirest after mine iniquity, and searchest after my sin? <hi type="super">7</hi> Thou knowest that I am not wicked; and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none that can deliver out of thine hand. <div eID="gen9455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9456" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A passionate resolution to persist in his complaint, <reference osisRef="Job.10.1">v. 1</reference>. Being daunted with the dread of God's majesty, so that he could not plead his cause with him, he resolves to give himself some ease by giving vent to his resentments. He begins with vehement language: "<hi type="italic">My soul is weary of my life,</hi> weary of this body, and impatient to get clear of it, fallen out with life, and displeased at it, sick of it, and longing for death." Through the weakness of grace he went contrary to the dictates even of nature itself. We should act more like men did we act more like saints. Faith and patience would keep us from being weary of our lives (and <hi type="italic">cruel to them,</hi> as some read it), even when Providence has made them most wearisome to us; for that is to be weary of God's correction. Job, being weary of his life and having ease no other way, resolves to complain, resolves to speak. He will not give vent to his soul by violent hands, but he will give vent to the bitterness of his soul by violent words. Losers think they may have leave to speak; and unbridled passions, as well as unbridled appetites, are apt to think it an excuse for their excursions that they cannot help them: but what have we wisdom and grace for, but to keep the mouth as with a bridle? Job's corruption speaks here, yet grace puts in a word. 1. He will complain, but he will <hi type="italic">leave his complaint upon himself.</hi> He would not impeach God, nor charge him with unrighteousness or unkindness; but, though he knew not particularly the ground of God's controversy with him and the cause of action, yet, in the general, he would suppose it to be in himself and willingly bear all the blame. 2. He will speak, but it shall be the <hi type="italic">bitterness of his soul</hi> that he will express, not his settled judgment. If I speak amiss, it is <hi type="italic">not I, but sin that dwells in me,</hi> not my soul, but its bitterness. <div eID="gen9456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9457" type="x-p"/> II. A humble petition to God. He will speak, but the first word shall be a prayer, and, as I am willing to understand it, it is a good prayer, <reference osisRef="Job.10.2">v. 2</reference>. 1. That he might be delivered from the sting of his afflictions, which is sin: "<hi type="italic">Do not condemn me;</hi> do not separate me for ever from thee. Though I lie under the cross, let me not lie under the curse; though I smart by the rod of a Father, let me not be cut off by the sword of a Judge. Thou dost correct me; I will bear that as well as I can; but O do not condemn me!" It is the comfort of those who are in Christ Jesus that, though they are in affliction, there is <hi type="italic">no condemnation to them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.1">Rom. viii. 1</reference>. Nay, they are <hi type="italic">chastened of the Lord that they may not be condemned with the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.32">1 Cor. xi. 32</reference>. This therefore we should deprecate above any thing else, when we are in affliction. "However thou art pleased to deal with me, Lord, do not condemn me; my friends condemn me, but do not thou." 2. That he might be made acquainted with the true cause of his afflictions, and that is sin too: Lord, <hi type="italic">show me wherefore thou contendest with me.</hi> When God afflicts us he contends with us, and when he contends with us there is always a reason. He is never angry without a cause, though we are; and it is desirable to know what the reason is, that we may repent of, mortify, and forsake the sin for which God has a controversy with us. In enquiring it out, let conscience have leave to do its office and to deal faithfully with us, as <reference osisRef="Gen.42.21">Gen. xlii. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen9457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9458" type="x-p"/> III. A peevish expostulation with God concerning his dealings with him. Now he speaks in the bitterness of his soul indeed, not without some ill-natured reflections upon the righteousness of his God. <div eID="gen9458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9459" type="x-p"/> 1. He thinks it unbecoming the goodness of God, and the mercifulness of his nature, to deal so hardly with his creature as to lay upon him more than he can bear (<reference osisRef="Job.10.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Is it good unto thee that thou shouldst oppress?</hi> No, certainly it is not; what he approves not in men (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.34-Lam.3.36">Lam. iii. 34-36</reference>) he will not do himself. "Lord, in dealing with me, thou seemest to oppress thy subject, to despise thy workmanship, and to countenance thy enemies. Now, Lord, what is the meaning of this? Such is thy nature that this cannot be a pleasure to thee; and such is thy name that it cannot be an honour to thee. Why then dealest thou thus with me? <hi type="italic">What profit is there in my blood?</hi>" Far be it from Job to think that God did him wrong, but he is quite at a loss how to reconcile his providences with his justice, as good men have often been, and must wait until the day shall declare it. Let us therefore now harbour no hard thoughts of God, because we shall then see there was no cause for them. <div eID="gen9459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9460" type="x-p"/> 2. He thinks it unbecoming the infinite knowledge of God to put his prisoner thus upon the rack, as it were, by torture, to extort a confession from him, <reference osisRef="Job.10.4-Job.10.6">v. 4-6</reference>. (1.) He is sure that God does not discover things, nor judge of them, as men do: He has not <hi type="italic">eyes of flesh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.10.4">v. 4</reference>), for he is a Spirit. Eyes of flesh cannot see in the dark, but darkness hides not from God. Eyes of flesh are but in one place at a time, and can see but a little way; but the <hi type="italic">eyes of the Lord are in every place,</hi> and <hi type="italic">run to and fro through the whole earth.</hi> Many things are hidden from eyes of flesh, the most curious and piercing; <hi type="italic">there is a path which even the vulture's eye has not seen:</hi> but nothing is, or can be, hidden from the eye of God, to which all things are naked and open. Eyes of flesh see the outward appearance only, and may be imposed upon by a <hi type="italic">deceptio visus—an illusion of the senses;</hi> but God sees every thing truly. His sight cannot be deceived, for he tries the heart, and is a witness to the thoughts and intents of that. Eyes of flesh discover things gradually, and, when we gain the sight of one thing, we lose the sight of another; but God sees every thing at one view. Eyes of flesh are soon tired, must be closed every night but the keeper of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps, nor does his sight ever decay. <hi type="italic">God sees not as man sees,</hi> that is, he does not judge as man judges, at the best <hi type="italic">secundum allegata et probata—according to what is alleged and proved,</hi> as the thing appears rather than as it is, and too often according to the bias of the affections, passions, prejudices, and interest; <hi type="italic">but we are sure that the judgment of God is according to truth,</hi> and that he knows truth, not by information, but by his own inspection. Men discover secret things by search, and examination of witnesses, comparing evidence and giving conjectures upon it, wheedling or forcing the parties concerned to confess; but God needs not any of these ways of discovery: <hi type="italic">he sees not as man sees.</hi> (2.) He is sure that as God is not short-sighted, like man, so he is not short-lived (<reference osisRef="Job.10.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Are thy days as the days of man,</hi> few and evil? Do they roll on in succession, or are they subject to change, like the days of man? No, by no means." Men grow wiser by experience and more knowing by daily observation; with them truth is the daughter of time, and therefore they must take time for their searches, and, if one experiment fail, must try another. But it is not so with God; to him nothing is past, nothing future, but every thing present. The days of time, by which the life of man is measured, are nothing to the years of eternity, in which the life of God is wrapped up. (3.) He therefore thinks it strange that God should thus prolong his torture, and continue him under the confinement of this affliction, and neither bring him to a trial nor grant him a release, as if he must take time to <hi type="italic">enquire after his iniquity</hi> and use means to <hi type="italic">search after his sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.10.6">v. 6</reference>. Not as if Job thought that God did thus torment him that he might find occasion against him; but his dealings with him had such an aspect, which was dishonourable to God, and would tempt men to think him a hard master. "Now, Lord, if thou wilt not consult my comfort, consult thy own honour; do something <hi type="italic">for thy great name,</hi> and <hi type="italic">do not disgrace the throne of thy glory,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Jer.14.21">Jer. xiv. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen9460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9461" type="x-p"/> 3. He thinks it looked like an abuse of his omnipotence to keep a poor prisoner in custody, whom he knew to be innocent, only because there was none that could deliver him out of his hand (<reference osisRef="Job.10.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou knowest that I am not wicked.</hi> He had already owned himself a sinner, and guilty before God; but he here stands to it that he was not wicked, not devoted to sin, not an enemy to God, not a dissembler in his religion, that <hi type="italic">he had not wickedly departed from his God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.21">Ps. xviii. 21</reference>. "<hi type="italic">But there is none that can deliver out of thy hand,</hi> and therefore there is no remedy; I must be content to lie there, waiting thy time, and throwing myself on thy mercy, in submission to thy sovereign will." Here see, (1.) What ought to quiet us under our troubles—that it is to no purpose to contend with Omnipotence. (2.) What will abundantly comfort us—if we are able to appeal to God, as Job here, "Lord, <hi type="italic">thou knowest that I am not wicked.</hi> I cannot say that l am not wanting, or I am not weak; but, through grace, I can say, <hi type="italic">I am not wicked:</hi> thou knowest I am not, for <hi type="italic">thou knowest I love thee.</hi>"
entries.0e7c6ad32d41a7e86adac0203c6905eb3c64112e: <div eID="gen9461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9462" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Thine hands have made me and fashioned me together round about; yet thou dost destroy me. <hi type="super">9</hi> Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me as the clay; and wilt thou bring me into dust again? <hi type="super">10</hi> Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese? <hi type="super">11</hi> Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews. 12 Thou hast granted me life and favour, and thy visitation hath preserved my spirit. <hi type="super">13</hi> And these <hi type="italic">things</hi> hast thou hid in thine heart: I know that this <hi type="italic">is</hi> with thee. <div eID="gen9462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9463" type="x-p"/> In these verses we may observe, <div eID="gen9463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9464" type="x-p"/> I. How Job eyes God as his Creator and preserver, and describes his dependence upon him as the author and upholder of his being. This is one of the first things we are all concerned to know and consider. <div eID="gen9464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9465" type="x-p"/> 1. That God made us, he, and not our parents, who were only the instruments of his power and providence in our production. <hi type="italic">He made us, and not we ourselves. His hands have made and fashioned</hi> these bodies of ours and every part of them (<reference osisRef="Job.10.8">v. 8</reference>), and they are <hi type="italic">fearfully and wonderfully made.</hi> The soul also, which animates the body, is his gift. Job takes notice of both here. (1.) The body is <hi type="italic">made as the clay</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.10.9">v. 9</reference>), cast into shape, into this shape, as the clay is formed into a vessel, according to the skill and will of the potter. We are earthen vessels, mean in our original, and soon broken in pieces, made <hi type="italic">as the clay. Let not</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">the thing formed say unto him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus?</hi> We must not be proud of our bodies, because the matter is from the earth, yet not dishonour our bodies, because the mould and shape are from the divine wisdom. The formation of human bodies in the womb is described by an elegant similitude (<reference osisRef="Job.10.10">v. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou hast poured me out like milk, which is coagulated into cheese</hi>), and by an induction of some particulars, <reference osisRef="Job.10.11">v. 11</reference>. Though we come into the world naked, yet the body is itself both clothed and armed. The skin and flesh are its clothing; the bones and sinews are its armour, not offensive, but defensive. The vital parts, the heart and lungs, are thus clothed, not to be seen—thus fenced, not to be hurt. The admirable structure of human bodies is an illustrious instance of the wisdom, power, and goodness of the Creator. What a pity is it that these bodies should be instruments of unrighteousness which are capable of being temples of the Holy Ghost! (2.) The soul is the life, the soul is the man, and this is the gift of God: <hi type="italic">Thou hast granted me life,</hi> breathed into me the breath of life, without which the body would be but a worthless carcase. God is the Father of spirits: he made us living souls, and endued us with the power of reason; he gave us <hi type="italic">life and favour,</hi> and life is a favour—a great favour, more than meat, more than raiment—a distinguishing favour, a favour that puts us into a capacity of receiving other favours. Now Job was in a better mind than he was when he quarrelled with life as a burden, and asked, <hi type="italic">Why died I not from the womb?</hi> Or by life and favour may be meant life and all the comforts of life, referring to his former prosperity. Time was when he walked in the light of the divine favour, and thought, as David, that through that favour his mountain stood strong. <div eID="gen9465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9466" type="x-p"/> 2. That God maintains us. Having lighted the lamp of life, he does not leave it to burn upon its own stock, but continually supplies it with fresh oil: "<hi type="italic">Thy visitation has preserved my spirit,</hi> kept me alive, protected me from the adversaries of life, the death we are in the midst of and the dangers we are continually exposed to, and blessed me with all the necessary supports of life and the daily supplies it needs and craves." <div eID="gen9466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9467" type="x-p"/> II. How he pleads this with God, and what use he makes of it. He reminds God of it (<reference osisRef="Job.10.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me.</hi> What then? Why, 1. "Thou hast made me, and therefore thou hast a perfect knowledge of me (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.1-Ps.139.13">Ps. cxxxix. 1-13</reference>), and needest not to examine me by scourging, nor to put me upon the rack for the discovery of what is within me." 2. "Thou hast made me, as the clay, by an act of sovereignty; and wilt thou by a like act of sovereignty unmake me again? If so, I must submit." 3. "Wilt thou destroy the work of thy own hands?" It is a plea the saints have often used in prayer, <hi type="italic">We are the clay and thou our potter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.64.8">Isa. lxiv. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thy hands have made me and fashioned me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.73">Ps. cxix. 73</reference>. So here, <hi type="italic">Thou madest me;</hi> and wilt thou destroy me (<reference osisRef="Job.10.8">v. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">wilt thou bring me into dust again?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.10.9">v. 9</reference>. "Wilt thou not pity me? Wilt thou not spare and help me, and stand by <hi type="italic">the work of thy own hands?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.138.8">Ps. cxxxviii. 8</reference>. Thou madest me, and knowest my strength; wilt thou then suffer me to be pressed above measure? Was I made to be made miserable? Was I preserved only to be reserved for these calamities?" If we plead this with ourselves as an inducement to duty, "God made me and maintains me, and therefore I will serve him and submit to him," we may plead it with God as an argument for mercy: <hi type="italic">Thou hast made me,</hi> new—make me; <hi type="italic">I am thine, save me.</hi> Job knew not how to reconcile God's former favours and his present frowns, but concludes (<reference osisRef="Job.10.13">v. 13</reference>), "<hi type="italic">These things hast thou hidden in thy heart.</hi> Both are according to the counsel of thy own will, and therefore undoubtedly consistent, however they seem." When God thus strangely changes his way, though we cannot account for it, we are bound to believe there are good reasons for it hidden in his heart, which will be manifested shortly. It is not with us, or in our reach, to assign the cause, but I <hi type="italic">know that this is with thee.</hi> Known unto God are all his works.
entries.8ad339730240007d64fb587b1fbbb016408d4dd9: <div eID="gen9467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9468" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> If I sin, then thou markest me, and thou wilt not acquit me from mine iniquity. <hi type="super">15</hi> If I be wicked, woe unto me; and <hi type="italic">if</hi> I be righteous, <hi type="italic">yet</hi> will I not lift up my head. <hi type="italic">I am</hi> full of confusion; therefore see thou mine affliction; <hi type="super">16</hi> For it increaseth. Thou huntest me as a fierce lion: and again thou showest thyself marvellous upon me. 17 Thou renewest thy witnesses against me, and increasest thine indignation upon me; changes and war <hi type="italic">are</hi> against me. 18 Wherefore then hast thou brought me forth out of the womb? Oh that I had given up the ghost, and no eye had seen me! 19 I should have been as though I had not been; I should have been carried from the womb to the grave. <hi type="super">20</hi> <hi type="italic">Are</hi> not my days few? cease <hi type="italic">then, and</hi> let me alone, that I may take comfort a little, <hi type="super">21</hi> Before I go <hi type="italic">whence</hi> I shall not return, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the land of darkness and the shadow of death; <hi type="super">22</hi> A land of darkness, as darkness <hi type="italic">itself; and</hi> of the shadow of death, without any order, and <hi type="italic">where</hi> the light <hi type="italic">is</hi> as darkness. <div eID="gen9468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9469" type="x-p"/> Here we have, <div eID="gen9469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9470" type="x-p"/> I. Job's passionate complaints. On this harsh and unpleasant string he harps much, in which, though he cannot be justified, he may be excused. He complained not for nothing, as the murmuring Israelites, but had cause to complain. If we think it looks ill in him, let it be a warning to us to keep our temper better. <div eID="gen9470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9471" type="x-p"/> 1. He complains of the strictness of God's judgment and the rigour of his proceedings against him, and is ready to call it <hi type="italic">summum jus—justice bordering on severity.</hi> That he took all advantages against him: "<hi type="italic">If I sin, then thou markest me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.10.14">v. 14</reference>. (1.) If I do but take one false step, misplace a word, or cast a look awry, I shall be sure to hear of it. Conscience, thy deputy, will be sure to upbraid me with it, and to tell me that this gripe, this twitch of pain, is to punish me for that." If God should thus mark iniquities, we should be undone; but we must acknowledge the contrary, that, though we sin, God does not deal in extremity with us. (2.) That he prosecuted those advantages to the utmost: <hi type="italic">Thou wilt not acquit me from my iniquity.</hi> While his troubles he could not take the comfort of his pardon, nor hear that voice of joy and gladness; so hard is it to see love in God's heart when we see frowns in his face and a rod in his hand. (3.) That, whatever was his character, his case at present was very uncomfortable, <reference osisRef="Job.10.15">v. 15</reference>. [1.] If he be wicked, he is certainly undone in the other world: <hi type="italic">If I be wicked, woe to me.</hi> Note, A sinful state is a woeful state. This we should each of us believe, as Job here, with application to ourselves: "<hi type="italic">If I be wicked,</hi> though prosperous and living in pleasure, yet woe to me." Some especially have reason to dread double woes if they be wicked. "I that have knowledge, that have made a great profession of religion, that have been so often under strong convictions, and have made so many fair promises—I that was born of such good parents, blessed with a good education, that have lived in good families, and long enjoyed the means of grace—<hi type="italic">if I be wicked, woe,</hi> and a thousand woes, <hi type="italic">to me.</hi>" [2.] If he be <hi type="italic">righteous,</hi> yet he dares not <hi type="italic">lift up his head,</hi> dares not answer as before, <reference osisRef="Job.9.15">ch. ix. 15</reference>. He is so oppressed and overwhelmed with his troubles that he cannot look up with any comfort or confidence. Without were fightings, within were fears; so that, between both, he was full of confusion, not only confusion of face for the disgrace he was brought down to and the censures of his friends, but confusion of spirit; his mind was in a constant hurry, and he was almost distracted, <reference osisRef="Ps.88.15">Ps. lxxxviii. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen9471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9472" type="x-p"/> 2. He complains of the severity of the execution. God (he thought) did not only punish him for every failure, but punish him in a high degree, <reference osisRef="Job.10.16-Job.10.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. His affliction was, (1.) Grievous, very grievous, marvellous, exceedingly marvellous. God <hi type="italic">hunted him</hi> as a lion, <hi type="italic">as a fierce lion</hi> hunts and runs down his prey. God was not only strange to him, but <hi type="italic">showed himself marvellous upon him,</hi> by bringing him into uncommon troubles and so making him prodigy, a wonder unto many. All wondered that God would inflict and that Job could bear so much. That which made his afflictions most grievous was that he felt God's <hi type="italic">indignation</hi> in them; it was this that made them taste so bitter and lie so heavy. They were God's <hi type="italic">witnesses</hi> against him, tokens of his displeasure; this made the sores of his body wounds in his spirit. (2.) It was growing, still growing worse and worse. This he insists much upon; when he hoped the tide would turn, and begin to ebb, still it flowed higher and higher. His affliction increased, and God's indignation in the affliction. He found himself no better, no way better. These witnesses were renewed against him, that, if one did not reach to convict him, another might. <hi type="italic">Changes and war</hi> were against him. If there was any change with him, it was not for the better; still he was kept in a state of war. As long as we are here in this world we must expect that the clouds will return after the rain, and perhaps the sorest and sharpest trials may be reserved for the last. God was at war with him, and it was a great change. He did not use to be so, which aggravated the trouble and made it truly marvellous. God usually shows himself kind to his people; if at any time he shows himself otherwise, it is <hi type="italic">his strange work, his strange act,</hi> and he does in it show himself marvellous. <div eID="gen9472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9473" type="x-p"/> 3. He complains of his life, and that ever he was born to all this trouble and misery (<reference osisRef="Job.10.18-Job.10.19">v. 18, 19</reference>): "If this was designed for my lot, <hi type="italic">why was I brought out of the womb,</hi> and not smothered there, or stifled in the birth?" This was the language of his passion, and it was a relapse into the same sin he fell into before. He had just now called life a <hi type="italic">favour</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.10.12">v. 12</reference>), yet now he calls it a <hi type="italic">burden,</hi> and quarrels with God for giving it, or rather laying it upon him. Mr. Caryl gives this a good turn in favour of Job. "We may charitably suppose," says he, "that what troubled Job was that he was in a condition of life which (as he conceived) hindered the main end of his life, which was the glorifying of God. His harp was hung on the willow-trees, and he was quite out of tune for praising God. Nay, he feared lest his troubles should reflect dishonour upon God and give occasion to his enemies to blaspheme; and therefore he wishes, <hi type="italic">O that I had given up the ghost!</hi> A godly man reckons that he lives to no purpose if he do not live to the praise and glory of God." If that was his meaning, it was grounded on a mistake; for we may <hi type="italic">glorify the Lord in the fires.</hi> But this use we may make of it, not to be over-fond of life, since the case has been such sometimes, even with wise and good men, that they have complained of it. Why should we dread giving up the ghost, or covet to be seen of men, since the time may come when we may be ready to wish we had given up the ghost and no eye had seen us? Why should we inordinately lament the death of our children in their infancy, that <hi type="italic">are as if they had not been,</hi> and are <hi type="italic">carried from the womb to the grave,</hi> when perhaps we ourselves may sometimes wish it had been our own lot? <div eID="gen9473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9474" type="x-p"/> II. Job's humble requests. He prays, 1. That God would <hi type="italic">see his affliction</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.10.15">v. 15</reference>), take cognizance of his case, and take it into his compassionate consideration. Thus David prays (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.18">Ps. xxv. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">Look upon my affliction and my pain.</hi> Thus we should, in our troubles, refer ourselves to God, and may comfort ourselves with this, that he knows our souls in adversity. 2. That God would grant him some ease. If he could not prevail for the removal of his trouble, yet might he not have some intermission? "Lord, let me not be always upon the rack, always in extremity: <hi type="italic">O let me alone, that I may take comfort a little!</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.10.20">v. 20</reference>. Grant me some respite, some breathing-time, some little enjoyment of myself." This he would reckon a great favour. Those that are not duly thankful for constant ease should think how welcome one hour's ease would be if they were in constant pain. Two things he pleads:—(1.) That life and its light were very short: "<hi type="italic">Are not my days few?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.10.20">v. 20</reference>. Yes, certainly they are, very few. Lord, let them not be all miserable, all in the extremity of misery. I have but a little time to live; let me have some comfort of life while it does last." This plea fastens on the goodness of God's nature, the consideration of which is very comfortable to an afflicted spirit. And, if we would use this as a plea with God for mercy ("<hi type="italic">Are not my days few?</hi> Lord, pity me"), we should use it as a plea with ourselves, to quicken us to duty: "<hi type="italic">Are not my days few?</hi> Then it concerns me to redeem time, to improve opportunities, what my hand finds to do to do it with all my might, that I may be ready for the days of eternity, which shall be many." (2.) That death and its darkness were very near and would be very long (<reference osisRef="Job.10.21-Job.10.22">v. 21, 22</reference>): "Lord, give me some ease before I die," that is, "lest I die of my pain." Thus David pleads (<reference osisRef="Ps.13.3">Ps. xiii. 3</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Lest I sleep the sleep of death,</hi> and then it will be too late to expect relief; for <hi type="italic">wilt thou show wonders to the dead?</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.88.10">Ps. lxxxviii. 10</reference>. "Let me have a little comfort before I die, that I may take leave of this world calmly, and not in such confusion as I am now in." Thus earnest should we be for grace, and thus we should plead, "Lord, renew me in the inward man; Lord, sanctify me before I die, for otherwise it will never be done." See how he speaks here of the state of the dead. [1.] It is a fixed state, whence we shall not return ever again to live such a life as we now live, <reference osisRef="Job.7.10">ch. vii. 10</reference>. At death we must bid a final farewell to this world. The body must then be laid where it will lie long, and the soul adjudged to that state in which it must be for ever. That had need be well done which is to be done but once, and done for eternity. [2.] It is a very melancholy state; so it appears to us. Holy souls, at death, remove to a land of light, where there is no death; but their bodies they leave to a <hi type="italic">land of darkness and the shadow of death.</hi> He heaps up expressions here of the same import to show that he has as dreadful apprehensions of death and the grave as other men naturally have, so that it was only the extreme misery he was in that made him wish for it. Come and let us look a little into the grave, and we shall find, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That there is no order there: it is <hi type="italic">without any order,</hi> perpetual night, and no succession of day. All there lie on the same level, and there is no distinction between prince and peasant, but <hi type="italic">the servant is</hi> there <hi type="italic">free from his master,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.3.19">ch. iii. 19</reference>. No order is observed in bringing people to the grave, not the eldest first, not the richest, not the poorest, and yet every one in his own order, the order appointed by the God of life. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That there is no light there. In the grave there is thick darkness, darkness that cannot be felt indeed, yet cannot but be feared by those that enjoy the light of life. In the grave there is no knowledge, no comfort, no joy, no praising God, no working out our salvation, and therefore no light. Job was so much ashamed that others should see his sores, and so much afraid to see them himself, that the darkness of the grave, which would hide them and huddle them up, would upon that account be welcome to him. Darkness comes upon us; and therefore let us walk and work while we have the light with us. The grave being a land of darkness, it is well we are carried thither with our eyes closed, and then it is all one. The grave is a land of darkness to man; our friends that have gone thither we reckon removed into darkness, <reference osisRef="Ps.88.18">Ps. lxxxviii. 18</reference>. But that it is not so to God will appear by this, that the dust of the bodies of the saints, though scattered, though mingled with other dust, will none of it be lost, for God's eye is upon every grain of it and it shall be forth-coming in the great day.  <chapter eID="Job.10"/> <div eID="gen9474" type="x-p"/>

entries.46d6312eed2e8fa20c22dadfc2d60eb44f0dc672: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4653"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.10.1-Job.10.22">Job 10:1-22</reference>. Job's Reply to Bildad Continued.</title> <div sID="gen6744" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4653"/><hi type="bold">1. leave my complaint upon myself--</hi>rather, "I will give loose to my complaint" (<reference osisRef="Job.7.11">Job 7:11</reference>). <div eID="gen6744" type="x-p"/>
entries.85cd610b7312bb095c8f7c86aacb053f85466135: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4654"/><div sID="gen6745" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4654"/><hi type="bold">2. show me, &c.--</hi>Do not, by virtue of Thy mere sovereignty, treat me as guilty without showing me the reasons. <div eID="gen6745" type="x-p"/>
entries.51da5ef9b9e38b471ba1bd420c931ac4c8e8f468: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4655"/><div sID="gen6746" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4655"/>3. Job is unwilling to think God can have pleasure in using His power to "oppress" the weak, and to treat man, the work of His own hands, as of no value (<reference osisRef="Job.10.8">Job 10:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.138.8">Psa 138:8</reference>).<div eID="gen6746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shine upon--</hi>favor with prosperity (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.2">Psa 50:2</reference>). <div eID="gen6747" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f584bfa5fc363ed595b14e5170985a7d97524a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4656"/><div sID="gen6748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4656"/>4-6. Dost Thou see as feebly as man? that is, with the same uncharitable eye, as, for instance, Job's friends? Is Thy time as short? Impossible! Yet one might think, from the rapid succession of Thy strokes, that Thou hadst no time to spare in overwhelming me. <div eID="gen6748" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae21fa32fafb41f68bdd619266702ca652c3b05a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4657"/><div sID="gen6749" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4657"/>7. "Although Thou (the Omniscient) knowest," &c. (connected with <reference osisRef="Job.10.6">Job 10:6</reference>), "Thou searchest after my sin."<div eID="gen6749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and ... that none that can deliver out of thine hand--</hi>Therefore Thou hast no need to deal with me with the rapid violence which man would use (see <reference osisRef="Job.10.6">Job 10:6</reference>). <div eID="gen6750" type="x-p"/>
entries.47fb68b7a11de8413569d35dcc4910ffa6bd5921: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4658"/><div sID="gen6751" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4658"/><hi type="bold">8. Made--</hi>with pains; implying a work of difficulty and art; applying to God language applicable only to man.<div eID="gen6751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6752" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">together round about--</hi>implying that the human body is a complete unity, the parts of which on all sides will bear the closest scrutiny. <div eID="gen6752" type="x-p"/>
entries.23bbb105b010d467b8775f2b53b44a0693321b8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4659"/><div sID="gen6753" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4659"/><hi type="bold">9. clay--</hi><reference osisRef="Job.10.10">Job 10:10</reference> proves that the reference here is, not so much to the perishable nature of the materials, as to their wonderful fashioning by the divine potter. <div eID="gen6753" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ec79eabaea951f0ac0e1ff5b398e3697baccab7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4660"/><div sID="gen6754" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4660"/>10. In the organization of the body from its rude commencements, the original liquid gradually assumes a more solid consistency, like milk curdling into cheese (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.15">Psa 139:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.16">16</reference>). Science reveals that the chyle circulated by the lacteal vessels is the supply to every organ. <div eID="gen6754" type="x-p"/>
entries.16fab814f146bd099f42520b59b05e614304f4ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4661"/><div sID="gen6755" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4661"/><hi type="bold">11. fenced--</hi>or "inlaid" (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.15">Psa 139:15</reference>); "curiously wrought" [Umbreit]. In the foetus the skin appears first, then the flesh, then the harder parts. <div eID="gen6755" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a4680878306936d9976501264c7bfa1a38351cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4662"/><div sID="gen6756" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4662"/><hi type="bold">12. visitation--</hi>Thy watchful Providence.<div eID="gen6756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6757" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spirit--</hi>breath. <div eID="gen6757" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e7f36708c222643e408cfdf7a18f3b28fc162ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4663"/><div sID="gen6758" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4663"/><hi type="bold">13. is with thee--</hi>was Thy purpose. All God's dealings with Job in his creation, preservation, and present afflictions were part of His secret counsel (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.16">Psa 139:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.15.18">Ac 15:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11">Ec 3:11</reference>). <div eID="gen6758" type="x-p"/>
entries.2d79728ffec38e1acba322bfd7c414863b63d173: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4664"/><div sID="gen6759" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4664"/>14-15. Job is perplexed because God "marks" every sin of his with such ceaseless rigor. Whether "wicked" (godless and a hypocrite) or "righteous" (comparatively sincere), God condemns and punishes alike. <div eID="gen6759" type="x-p"/>
entries.176277960fa41898455a713435a728e01e11482d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4666"/><div sID="gen6762" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4666"/><hi type="bold">16. increaseth--</hi>rather, "(if) I lift up (my head) Thou wouldest hunt me," &c. [Umbreit].<div eID="gen6762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6763" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and again--</hi>as if a lion should not kill his prey at once, but come back and torture it again. <div eID="gen6763" type="x-p"/>
entries.3e4ff8bdd7e2c7c8312317a9944bdfe657456e59: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4667"/><div sID="gen6764" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4667"/><hi type="bold">17. witnesses--</hi>His accumulated trials were like a succession of witnesses brought up in proof of his guilt, to wear out the accused.<div eID="gen6764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">changes and war--</hi>rather, "(thou settest in array) against me host after host" (literally, "changes and a host," that is, a succession of hosts); namely, his afflictions, and then reproach upon reproach from his friends. <div eID="gen6765" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e19da2e11b6d3cf63c3895da9018c276cc2d2bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4668"/><div sID="gen6766" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4668"/>20. But, since I was destined from my birth to these ills, at least give me a little breathing time during the few days left me (<reference osisRef="Job.9.34">Job 9:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.21">13:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.39.13">Psa 39:13</reference>). <div eID="gen6766" type="x-p"/>
entries.e673cca732cb694dd6ab523ff8054e40d3948ef4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4669"/><div sID="gen6767" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4669"/>22. The ideas of order and light, disorder and darkness, harmonize (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.2">Ge 1:2</reference>). Three Hebrew words are used for darkness; in <reference osisRef="Job.10.21">Job 10:21</reference> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.1">1</reference>) the common word "darkness"; here (2) "a land of gloom" (from a Hebrew root, "to cover up"); (3) as "thick darkness" or blackness (from a root, expressing sunset). "Where the light thereof is like blackness." Its only sunshine is thick darkness. A bold figure of poetry. Job in a better frame has brighter thoughts of the unseen world. But his views at best wanted the definite clearness of the Christian's. Compare with his words here <reference osisRef="Rev.21.23">Re 21:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.5">22:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.10">2Ti 1:10</reference>. <chapter eID="Job.10"/>

entries.51c0477152011b8e32289af0e562ee993045450c: <div eID="gen16288" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16289" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16290" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16290" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16289" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16291" type="x-p"/> Job is weary of life, and expostulates with God, <reference osisRef="Job.10.1-Job.10.6">Job 10:1-6</reference>. He appeals to God for his innocence; and pleads on the weakness of his frame, and the manner of his formation, <reference osisRef="Job.10.7-Job.10.13">Job 10:7-13</reference>. Complains of his sufferings, and prays for respite, <reference osisRef="Job.10.14-Job.10.20">Job 10:14-20</reference>. Describes the state of the dead, <reference osisRef="Job.10.21">Job 10:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.10.22">Job 10:22</reference>. <div eID="gen16291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16292" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen16292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16293" type="x-p"/> My soul is weary of my life - Here is a proof that נפש nephesh does not signify the animal life, but the soul or immortal mind, as distinguished from חי chai, that animal life; and is a strong proof that Job believed in the distinction between these two principles; was no materialist; but, on the contrary, credited the proper immortality of the soul. This is worthy of observation. See <reference osisRef="Job.12.10">Job 12:10</reference>. <div eID="gen16293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16294" type="x-p"/> I will leave my complaint - I still charge myself with the cause of my own calamities; and shall not charge my Maker foolishly: but I must deplore my wretched and forlorn state.
entries.3aba8be425bd09a63dc3b7f93c05e4d29bdbaafc: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen16294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16295" type="x-p"/> Do not condemn me - Let me not be afflicted in thy wrath. <div eID="gen16295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16296" type="x-p"/> Show me wherefore thou contendest - If I am afflicted because of my sins, show me what that sin is. God never afflicts but for past sin, or to try his followers; or for the greater manifestation of his grace in their support and deliverance.
entries.5936b494ccf37d27bb6a316730e17ccc7e787a43: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen16296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16297" type="x-p"/> Is it good unto thee - Surely it can be no gratification to thee to distress the children of men, as if thou didst despise the work of thy own hands. <div eID="gen16297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16298" type="x-p"/> And shine upon the counsel - For by my afflictions the harsh judgments of the wicked will appear to be confirmed: viz., that God regards not his most fervent worshippers; and it is no benefit to lead a religious life.
entries.f2e7fd7b65943ef833adf3025a8955fb183b7d13: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen16298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16299" type="x-p"/> Hast thou eyes of flesh! - Dost thou judge as man judges? <div eID="gen16299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16300" type="x-p"/> Illustrated by the next clause, Seest thou as man seeth?
entries.bec70ab2a3b177bee6f9cee08b45b9da5b2f8420: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen16300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16301" type="x-p"/> Are thy days as the days of man - אנוש enosh, wretched, miserable man. Thy years as man's days; גבר gaber, the strong man. Thou art not short-lived, like man in his present imperfect state; nor can the years of the long-lived patriarchs be compared with thine. The difference of the phraseology in the original justifies this view of the subject. Man in his low estate cannot be likened unto thee; nor can he in his greatest excellence, though made in thy own image and likeness, be compared to thee.
entries.742c0ee12922ce11a474952a7aadbcf0a017f650: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen16301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16302" type="x-p"/> That thou inquirest - Is it becoming thy infinite dignity to concern thyself so much with the affairs or transgressions of a despicable mortal? A word spoken in the heart of most sinners.
entries.c0cb919fb7d1d74f5a51777787941a9b386cbec9: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen16302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16303" type="x-p"/> Thou knowest that I am not wicked - While thou hast this knowledge of me and my conduct, why appear to be sifting me as if in order to find out sin; and though none can be found, treating me as though I were a transgressor?
entries.b7a016056cf73170aa8accbc9913d841fd37620a: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen16303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16304" type="x-p"/> Thine hands have made me - Thou art well acquainted with human nature, for thou art its author. <div eID="gen16304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16305" type="x-p"/> And fashioned me together round about - All my powers and faculties have been planned and executed by thyself. It is thou who hast refined the materials out of which I have been formed, and modified them into that excellent symmetry and order in which they are now found; so that the union and harmony of the different parts, (יחד yachad), and their arrangement and completion, (סביב sabib), proclaim equally thy wisdom, skill, power, and goodness. <div eID="gen16305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16306" type="x-p"/> Yet thou dost destroy me - ותבלעני vatteballeeni, "and thou wilt swallow me up." Men generally care for and prize those works on which they have spent most time, skill, and pains: but, although thou hast formed me with such incredible skill and labor, yet thou art about to destroy me! How dreadful an evil must sin be, when, on its account, God has pronounced the sentence of death on all mankind; and that body, so curiously and skilfully formed, must be decomposed, and reduced to dust!
entries.4705b5c968762fd0d493686479387bf7725f7883: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen16306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16307" type="x-p"/> Thou hast made me as the clay - Thou hast fashioned me, according to thy own mind, out of a mass of clay: after so much skill and pains expended, men might naturally suppose they were to have a permanent being; but thou hast decreed to turn them into dust!
entries.4e6ea64d759cbac5643cf3cf53a7207943951579: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen16307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16308" type="x-p"/> Hast thou not poured me out as milk - After all that some learned men have said on this subject, in order to confine the images here to simple nutrition, I am satisfied that generation is the true notion. Respicit ad fetus in matris utero primam formationem, quum in embryonem ex utriusque parentis semine coalescit - Ex semine liquido, lac quodammodo referente, me formasti - In interpretando, inquit Hieronymus, omnino his accedo qui de genitali semine accipiunt, quod ipsa tanquam natura emulget, ac dein concrescere in utero ad coalescere jubet. I make no apology for leaving this untranslated. The different expressions in this and the following verse are very appropriate: the pouring out like milk-coagulating, clothing with skin and flesh, fencing with bones and sinews, are well imagined, and delicately, and at the same time forcibly, expressed. If I believed that Job referred to nutrition, which I do not, I might speak of the chyle, the chylopoietic organs, the lacteal vessels, and the generation of all the solids and fluids from this substance, which itself is derived from the food taken into the stomach. But this process, properly speaking, does not take place till the human being is brought into the world, it being previously nourished by the mother by means of the funis umbilicus, without that action of the stomach by which the chyle is prepared.
entries.fce80cc577deab10bff5643cc5fa03bb429a6e30: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen16308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16309" type="x-p"/> Thou hast granted me life and favorer - Thou hast brought me from my mother's womb; given me an actual existence among men; by thy favor or mercy thou hast provided me with the means of life; and thy visitation - thy continual providential care, has preserved me in life - has given me the air I breathe, and furnished me with those powers which enable me to respire it as an agent and preserver of life. It is by God's continued visitation or influence that the life of any man is preserved; in him we live, move, and have our being.
entries.4ac0280a24e3ba58c0ffab4a352787b39119bbbb: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen16309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16310" type="x-p"/> And these things hast thou hid in thine heart - Thou hast had many gracious purposes concerning me which thou hast not made known; but thy visitations and mercy are sufficient proofs of kindness towards me; though for purposes unknown to me thou hast sorely afflicted me, and continuest to treat me as an enemy.
entries.2189ec9c3fcd7196cc92a6df0fa716be106a0829: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen16310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16311" type="x-p"/> If I sin - From thee nothing can be hidden; if I sin, thou takest account of the transgression, and canst not hold me for innocent when thou knowest I am guilty.
entries.fcf5e0814e788398e279ea2331521686acc9a1c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen16311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16312" type="x-p"/> If I be wicked - I must meet with that punishment that is due to the workers of iniquity. <div eID="gen16312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16313" type="x-p"/> If I be righteous - I am only in the state which my duty to my Creator requires me to be in; and I cannot therefore suppose that on this account I can deserve any thing by way of favor from the justice of my Maker. <div eID="gen16313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16314" type="x-p"/> I am full of confusion - I am confounded at my state and circumstances. I know that thou art merciful, and dost not afflict willingly the children of men; I know I have not wickedly departed from thee; and yet I am treated by thee as if I were an apostate from every good. I am therefore full of confusion. See thou to my affliction; and bring me out of it in such a way as shall at once prove my innocence, the righteousness of thy ways, and the mercy of thy nature.
entries.042c2c3d61cf50a925130b0c30c6b580e8fe28bb: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen16314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16315" type="x-p"/> For it increaseth - Probably this refers to the affliction mentioned above, which is increased in proportion to its duration. Every day made his escape from such a load of evils less and less probable. <div eID="gen16315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16316" type="x-p"/> Thou huntest me as a fierce lion - As the hunters attack the king of beasts in the forest, so my friends attack me. They assail me on every side. <div eID="gen16316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16317" type="x-p"/> Thou showest thyself marvelous - Thy designs, thy ways, thy works, are all incomprehensible to me; thou dost both confound and overpower me. Mr. Good translates thus: - "For uprousing as a ravenous lion dost thou spring upon me. <div eID="gen16317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16318" type="x-p"/> And again thou showest over me thy vast power."
entries.0a713db2a9e8d1ed4732f4dba2796239d25bc2df: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen16318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16319" type="x-p"/> Thou renewest thy witnesses - In this speech of Job he is ever referring to trials in courts of judicature, and almost all his terms are forensic. Thou bringest witnesses in continual succession to confound and convict me. <div eID="gen16319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16320" type="x-p"/> Changes and war - I am as if attacked by successive troops; one company being wearied, another succeeds to the attack, so that I am harassed by continual warfare.
entries.c7c555336546ac8a80a5c7c685d2537fc071e94f: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen16320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16321" type="x-p"/> Wherefore then - Why didst thou give me a being, when thou didst foresee I should be exposed to such incredible hardships? See on <reference osisRef="Job.3.10">Job 3:10</reference> (note), etc.
entries.77f71ae1cf69be81e06f67f82428643116c09e0c: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen16321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16322" type="x-p"/> I should have been as though - Had I given up the ghost as soon as born, as I could not then have been conscious of existence, it would have been, as it respects myself, as though I had never been; being immediately transported from my mother's womb to the grave.
entries.bd185719b32668ea1b7c7f524cfebaf3ef045cd9: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen16322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16323" type="x-p"/> Are not my days few? - My life cannot be long; let me have a little respite before I die.
entries.78609767af6ff6b1ada0bc6bc06e719dfe042aa3: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen16323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16324" type="x-p"/> I shall not return - I shall not return again from the dust to have a dwelling among men. <div eID="gen16324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16325" type="x-p"/> To the land of darkness - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Job.3.5">Job 3:5</reference>. There are here a crowd of obscure and dislocated terms, admirably expressive of the obscurity and uncertainty of the subject. What do we know of the state of separate spirits? What do we know of the spiritual world? How do souls exist separate from their respective bodies? Of what are they capable and what is their employment? Who can answer these questions? Perhaps nothing can be said much better of the state than is here said, a land of obscurity, like darkness. The shadow of death - A place where death rules, over which he projects his shadow, intercepting every light of every kind of life. Without any order, ולא סדרים velo sedarim, having no arrangements, no distinctions of inhabitants; the poor and the rich are there, the master and his slave, the king and the beggar, their bodies in equal corruption and disgrace, their souls distinguished only by their moral character. Stripped of their flesh, they stand in their naked simplicity before God in that place.
entries.9f3e973baf793c6f5714a5078bb4187a38eae1d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen16325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16326" type="x-p"/> Where the light is as darkness - A palpable obscure: it is space and place, and has only such light or capability of distinction as renders "darkness visible." The following words of Sophocles convey the same idea: Ιω σκοτος εμοι φαος; "Thou darkness be my light." It is, as the Vulgate expresses it, Terra tenebrosa, et operta mortis caligine: Terra miseriae et tenebrarum, ubi umbra mortis, et nullus ordo, sed sempiternus horror inhabitat: "A murky land, covered with the thick darkness of death: a land of wretchedness and obscurities, where is the shadow of death, and no order, but sempiternal horror dwells everywhere." Or, as Coverdale expresses this last clause, Wheras is no ordre but terrible feare as in the darknesse. A duration not characterized or measured by any of the attributes of time; where there is no order of darkness and light, night and day, heat and cold, summer and winter. It is the state of the dead! The place of separate spirits! It is out of time, out of probation, beyond change or mutability. It is on the confines of eternity! But what is This? and where? Eternity! how can I form any conception of thee? In thee there is no order, no bounds, no substance, no progression, no change, no past, no present, no future! Thou art an indescribable something, to which there is no analogy in the compass of creation. Thou art infinity and incomprehensibility to all finite beings. Thou art what, living, I know not, and what I must die to know; and even then I shall apprehend no more of thee than merely that thou art E-T-E-R-N-I-T-Y!  <chapter eID="Job.10"/> <div eID="gen16326" type="x-p"/>

entries.e19efa8c964e81c27044ab2adb8f16dd9ad5aec9: <reference osisRef="Job.10.1-Job.2.1">Job 10:1-2   1</reference>  My soul is full of disgust with my life, <div eID="gen7224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7225" type="x-p"/> Therefore I will freely utter my complaint; <div eID="gen7225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7226" type="x-p"/> I will speak in the bitterness of my soul.   2  I will say to Eloah: Condemn me not; <div eID="gen7226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7227" type="x-p"/> Let me know wherefore Thou contendest with me! <div eID="gen7227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7228" type="x-p"/> His self-consciousness makes him desire that the possibility of answering for himself might be granted him; and since he is weary of life, and has renounced all claim for its continuance, he will at least give his complaints free course, and pray the Author of his sufferings that He would not permit him to die the death of the wicked, contrary to the testimony of his own conscience. נקטה is equivalent to נקטּה ot tnel, <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.9">Eze 6:9</reference>, after the usual manner of the contraction of double <hi type="italic">Ayin</hi> verbs (<reference osisRef="Gen.11.6-Gen.11.7">Gen 11:6-7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.3">Isa 19:3</reference>; Jdg 5:5; <reference osisRef="Ezek.41.7">Eze 41:7</reference>; vid., Ges. §67, rem. 11); it may nevertheless be derived directly from נקט, for this secondary verb formed from the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. נקט is supported by the Aramaic. In like manner, in <reference osisRef="Gen.17.11">Gen 17:11</reference> perhaps a secondary verb נמל, and certainly in <reference osisRef="Gen.9.19">Gen 9:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.23.3">Isa 23:3</reference> a secondary verb נפץ   (<reference osisRef="1Sam.13.11">1Sa 13:11</reference>), formed from the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. נפץ (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.18">Gen 10:18</reference>), is to be supposed; for the contraction of the <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi> form נקומה into נקמה is impossible; and the supposition which has been advanced, of a root פצץ = פוץ in the signification <hi type="italic">diffundere, dissipare</hi> is unnecessary. His soul is disgusted (<hi type="italic">fastidio affecta est</hi>, or <hi type="italic">fastidit</hi>) with his life, therefore he will give free course to his plaint (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.7.11">Job 7:11</reference>). עלי is not <hi type="italic">super</hi> or <hi type="italic">de</hi> <hi type="italic">me</hi>, but, as <reference osisRef="Job.30.16">Job 30:16</reference>, <hi type="italic">in me;</hi> it belongs to the Ego, as an expression of spontaneity: I in myself, since the Ego is the subject, ὑποκείμενον, of his individuality (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 151f.). The inner man is meant, which has the Ego over or in itself; from this the complaint shall issue forth as a stream without restraint; not, however, a mere gloomy lamentation over his pain, but a supplicatory complaint directed to God respecting the peculiar pang of his suffering, viz., this stroke which seems to come upon him from his Judge (ריב, <hi type="italic">seq. acc.,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Isa.27.8">Isa 27:8</reference>), without his being conscious of that for which he is accounted guilty.
entries.2ae2124bde4d13e859bfc77091592044f89219ad: <reference osisRef="Job.10.3-Job.7.3">Job 10:3-7   3</reference>  Doth it please Thee when Thou oppressest, <div eID="gen7228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7229" type="x-p"/> That Thou rejectest the work of Thy hands, <div eID="gen7229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7230" type="x-p"/> While Thou shinest upon the counsel of the wicked?   4  Hast Thou eyes of flesh, <div eID="gen7230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7231" type="x-p"/> Or seest Thou as a mortal seeth?   5  Are Thy days as the days of a mortal, <div eID="gen7231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7232" type="x-p"/> Or Thy years as man’s days,   6  That Thou seekest after my iniquity, <div eID="gen7232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7233" type="x-p"/> And searchest after my sin?   7  Although Thou knowest that I am not a wicked man, <div eID="gen7233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7234" type="x-p"/> And there is none that can deliver out of Thy hand. <div eID="gen7234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7235" type="x-p"/> There are three questions by which Job seeks to exhaust every possible way of accounting for his sufferings as coming from God. These attempts at explanation, however, are at once destroyed, because they proceed upon conceptions which are unworthy of God, and opposed to His nature. <hi type="italic">Firstly</hi>, Whether it gives Him pleasure (טּוב, agreeable, as <reference osisRef="Job.13.9">Job 13:9</reference>) when He oppresses, when He despises, i.e., keeps down forcibly or casts from Him as hateful (מאס, as <reference osisRef="Ps.89.39">Psa 89:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.54.6">Isa 54:6</reference>) the work of His hand; while, on the contrary, He permits light to shine from above upon the design of the wicked, i.e., favours it? Man is called the יגיע of the divine hands, as though he were elaborated by them, because at his origin (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Gen 2:7</reference>), the continuation of which is the development in the womb (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.15">Psa 139:15</reference>), he came into existence in a remarkable manner by the directly personal, careful, and, so to speak, skilful working of God. That it is the morally innocent which is here described, may be seen not only from the contrast (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.10.3">Job 10:3</reference></hi>), but also from the fact that he only can be spoken of as oppressed and rejected. Moreover, “the work of Thy hands” involves a negative reply to the question. Such an unloving mood of self-satisfaction is contrary to the bounty and beneficence of that love to which man owes his existence. <hi type="italic">Secondly</hi>, Whether God has eyes of flesh, i.e., of sense, which regard only the outward appearance, without an insight into the inner nature, or whether He sees as mortals see, i.e., judges, κατὰ τῆν σάρκα (Joh 8:15)? Mercier correctly: <hi type="italic">num ex facie judicas, ut affectibus ducaris more hominum.</hi> This question also supplies its own negative; it is based upon the thought that God lookest on the heart (<reference osisRef="1Sam.16.7">1Sa 16:7</reference>). <hi type="italic">Thirdly</hi>, Whether His life is like to the brevity of man’s life, so that He is not able to wait until a man’s sin manifests itself, but must institute such a painful course of investigation with him, in order to extort from him as quickly as possible a confession of it? Suffering appears here to be a means of inquisition, which is followed by the final judgment when the guilt is proved. What is added in <reference osisRef="Job.10.7">Job 10:7</reference> puts this supposition aside also as inconceivable. Such a mode of proceeding may be conceived of in a mortal ruler, who, on account of his short-sightedness, seeks to bring about by severe measures that which was at first only conjecture, and who, from the apprehension that he may not witness that vengeance in which he delights, hastens forward the criminal process as much as possible, in order that his victim may not escape him. God, however, to whom belongs absolute knowledge and absolute power, would act thus, although, etc. על, although, notwithstanding (proceeding from the signification, besides, <hi type="italic">insuper</hi>), as <reference osisRef="Job.17.16">Job 17:16</reference> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.9">Isa 53:9</reference>), Job 34:6. God knows even from the first that he (Job) will not appear as a guilty person (רשׁע, as in <reference osisRef="Job.9.29">Job 9:29</reference>); and however that may be, He is at all events sure of him, for nothing escapes the hand of God. <div eID="gen7235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7236" type="x-p"/> That operation of the divine love which is first echoed in “the labour of Thy hands,” is taken up in the following strophe, and, as Job contemplates it, his present lot seems to him quite incomprehensible.
entries.8b9cfc8caddb2d21aa8c4a5daaef6f50230a3969: Job 10:8-12   8  Thy hands have formed and perfected me <div eID="gen7236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7237" type="x-p"/> Altogether round about, and Thou hast now swallowed me up!   9  Consider now, that Thou has perfected me as clay, <div eID="gen7237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7238" type="x-p"/> And wilt Thou turn me again into dust? 10  Hast Thou not poured me out as milk, <div eID="gen7238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7239" type="x-p"/> And curdled me as curd? 11  With skin and flesh hast Thou clothed me, <div eID="gen7239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7240" type="x-p"/> And Thou hast intertwined me with bones and sinews; 12  Life and favour Thou hast shown me, <div eID="gen7240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7241" type="x-p"/> And thy care hath guarded my breath. <div eID="gen7241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7242" type="x-p"/> The development of the embryo was regarded by the Israelitish Chokma as one of the greatest mysteries (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.5">Ecc 11:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.2">2</reference> Macc. 7:22f.). There are two poetical passages which treat explicitly of this mysterious existence: this strophe of the book of Job, and the Psalm by David, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.13-Ps.139.16">Psa 139:13-16</reference> (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 210). The assertion of Scheuchzer, Hoffmann, and Oetinger, that these passages of Scripture “include, and indeed go beyond, all recent <hi type="italic">systemata generationis</hi>,” attributes to Scripture a design of imparting instruction, - a purpose which is foreign to it. Scripture nowhere attempts an analysis of the workings of nature, but only traces them back to their final cause. According to the view of Scripture, a creative act similar to the creation of Adam is repeated at the origin of each individual; and the continuation of development according to natural laws is not less the working of God than the creative planting of the very beginning. Thy hands, says Job, have formed (עצּב, to cut, carve, fashion; cognate are חצב, קצב, without the accompanying notion of toil, which makes this word specially appropriate, as describing the fashioning of the complicated nature of man) and perfected me. We do not translate: made; for עשׂה stands in the same relation to ברא and יצר as <hi type="italic">perficere</hi> to <hi type="italic">creare</hi> and <hi type="italic">fingere</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.2">Gen 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.7">Isa 43:7</reference>). יחד refers to the members of the body collectively, and סביב to the whole form. The perfecting as clay implies three things: the earthiness of the substance, the origin of man without his knowledge and co-operation, and the moulding of the shapeless substance by divine power and wisdom. The primal origin of man, <hi type="italic">de limo terrae</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.33.6">Job 33:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.139.15">Psa 139:15</reference>), is repeated in the womb. The figures which follow (<reference osisRef="Job.10.10">Job 10:10</reference>) describe this origin, which being obscure is all the more mysterious, and glorifies the power of God the more. The <hi type="italic">sperma</hi> is likened to milk; the חתּיך (used elsewhere of smelting), which Seb. Schmid rightly explains <hi type="italic">rem colliquatam fundere et immittere in formam aliquam</hi>, refers to the <hi type="italic">nisus formativus </hi>which dwells in it. The embryo which is formed from the <hi type="italic">sperma</hi> is likened to גּבינה, which means in all the Semitic dialects cheese (curd). “As whey” (Ewald, Hahn) is not suitable; whey does not curdle; in making cheese it is allowed to run off from the curdled milk. “As cream” (Schlottm.) is not less incorrect; cream is not lac <hi type="italic">coagulatum</hi>, which the word signifies. The embryo forming itself from the <hi type="italic">sperma</hi> is like milk which is curdled and beaten into shape. <div eID="gen7242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7243" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">consecutio temporum,</hi> moreover, must be observed here. It is, for example, incorrect to translate, with Ewald: Dost Thou not let me flow away like milk, etc. Job looks back to the beginning of his life; the four clauses, <reference osisRef="Job.10.10">Job 10:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.10.11">Job 10:11</reference>, under the control of the first two verbs (<reference osisRef="Job.10.8">Job 10:8</reference>), which influence the whole strophe, are also retrospective in meaning. The <hi type="italic">futt. </hi>are consequently like synchronous <hi type="italic">imperff.;</hi> as, then, <reference osisRef="Job.10.12">Job 10:12</reference> returns to <hi type="italic">perff.,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.10.11">Job 10:11</reference> describes the development of the embryo to the full-grown infant, on which Grotius remarks: <hi type="italic">Hic ordo est in genitura: primum pellicula fit, deinde in ea caro, duriora paulatim accedunt,</hi> and by <reference osisRef="Job.10.12">Job 10:12</reference>, the manifestations of divine goodness, not only in the womb, but from the beginning of life and onwards, are intended. The expression “Life and favour (this combination does not occur elsewhere) hast Thou done to me” is zeugmatic: He has given him life, and sustained that life amidst constant proofs of favour; His care has guarded the spirit (רוּח), by which his frame becomes a living and self-conscious being. This grateful retrospect is interspersed with painful reflections, in which Job gives utterance to his feeling of the contrast between the manifestation of the divine goodness which he had hitherto experienced and his present condition. As in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.10.8">Job 10:8</reference></hi>., ותּבלּעני, which Hirzel wrongly translates: and wilt now destroy me; it is rather: and hast now swallowed me up, i.e., drawn me down into destruction, as it were brought me to nought; or even, if in the <hi type="italic">fut. consec.,</hi> as is frequently the case, the consecutive and not the aorist signification preponderates: and now swallowest me up; and in <reference osisRef="Job.10.9">Job 10:9</reference> (where, though not clear from the syntax, it is clear from the substance that תשׁיבני is not to be understood as an imperfect, like the <hi type="italic">futt.</hi> in Job 10:10.): wilt Thou cause me to become dust again? The same tone is continued in the following strophe. Thus graciously has he been brought into being, and his life sustained, in order that he may come to such a terrible end.
entries.9ef4033fd67a6a5f95fbc6ec107b191a8e0c3d04: Job 10:13-17 13  And such Thou hast hidden in Thy heart, <div eID="gen7243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7244" type="x-p"/> I perceive that this was in Thy mind: 14  If I should sin, Thou wouldst take note of it, <div eID="gen7244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7245" type="x-p"/> And not acquit me of my iniquity. 15  If I should act wickedly, woe unto me! <div eID="gen7245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7246" type="x-p"/> And were I righteous, I should not lift up my head, <div eID="gen7246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7247" type="x-p"/> Being full of shame and conscious of my misery. 16  And were I to raise it, Thou wouldst hunt me as a lion, <div eID="gen7247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7248" type="x-p"/> And ever display on me Thy wondrous power, 17  Thou wouldst ever bring fresh witnesses against me, <div eID="gen7248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7249" type="x-p"/> And increase Thy wrath against me, <div eID="gen7249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7250" type="x-p"/> I should be compelled to withstand continuously advancing troops and a host. <div eID="gen7250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7251" type="x-p"/> This manifestation of divine goodness which Job has experienced from the earliest existence seems to him, as he compares his present lot of suffering with it, to have served as a veil to a hidden purpose of a totally opposite character. That purpose - to make this life, which has been so graciously called into existence and guarded thus far, the object of the severest and most condemning visitation - is now manifest. Both אלּה and זאת refer to what is to follow: עמּך זאת used of the thought conceived, the purpose cherished, as <reference osisRef="Job.23.14">Job 23:14</reference>; Job 27:11. All that follows receives a future colouring from this principal clause, “This is what Thou hadst designed to do,” which rules the strophe. Thus <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.10.14">Job 10:14</reference></hi> is to be rendered: If I had sinned, Thou wouldst have kept me in remembrance, properly <hi type="italic">custodies me,</hi> which is here equivalent to <hi type="italic">custoditurus eras me.</hi> שׁמר, with the acc. of the person, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.130.3">Psa 130:3</reference> (where it is followed by the acc. of the sin), is to be understood: to keep any one in remembrance, i.e., to mark him as sinful (Hirzel). This appears more appropriate than <hi type="italic">rigide observaturus eras me</hi> (Schlottm.). ושׁמרתני, according to Ges. §121, 4, might be taken for לי ושׁמרת (viz., חטּאתי); but this is unnecessary, and we have merely translated it thus for the sake of clearness. His infirmities must not be passed by unpunished; and if he should act wickedly (רשׁע, of malignant sin, in distinction from חטא), woe unto him (comp. οἰαί μοι, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.16">1Co 9:16</reference>). According to the construction referred to above, וצדקתי is <hi type="italic">praet. hypotheticum</hi> (Ges. §155, 4, <hi type="italic">a</hi>); and the conclusion follows without <hi type="italic">waw</hi> <hi type="italic">apodosis:</hi> If I had acted rightly, I should not have raised my head, being full of shame and conscious of my misery. The adjectives are not in apposition to ראשׁי (Böttcher), but describe the condition into which he would be brought, instead of being able (according to the ethical principle, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.7">Gen 4:7</reference>) to raise his head cheerfully. ראה <hi type="italic">constr</hi>. of ראה, as שׂבע or שׂבע. It is needless, with Pisc., Hirz., Böttch., and Ewald, to alter it to ראה, since ראה is verbal adjective like יפה, נכה, קשׁה. Moreover, וּראה cannot be imperative (Rosenm., De Wette); for although imperatives, joined by <hi type="italic">waw</hi> to sentences of a different construction, do occur (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.2">Psa 77:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.3">2Sa 21:3</reference>), such an exclamation would destroy the connection and tone of the strophe in the present case.
entries.9dc2e9641f725c3670675c8b55923945ffe4353d: Job 10:18-22 18  And wherefore hast Thou brought me forth out of the womb? <div eID="gen7251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7252" type="x-p"/> I should have expired, that no eye had seen me, 19  I should have been as though I had never been, <div eID="gen7252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7253" type="x-p"/> Carried from the womb to the grave. 20  Are not my days few? then cease <div eID="gen7253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7254" type="x-p"/> And turn from me, that I may become a little cheerful, 21  Before I go to return no more <div eID="gen7254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7255" type="x-p"/> Into the land of darkness and of the shadow of death, 22  The land of deep darkness like to midnight, <div eID="gen7255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7256" type="x-p"/> Of the shadow of death and of confusion, <div eID="gen7256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7257" type="x-p"/> And which is bright like midnight. <div eID="gen7257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7258" type="x-p"/> The question Wherefore? <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.10.18">Job 10:18</reference></hi>, is followed by <hi type="italic">futt</hi>. as <hi type="italic">modi conditionales</hi> (Ges. §127, 5) of that which would and should have happened, if God had not permitted him to be born alive: I should have expired, prop. I ought to have expired, being put back to the time of birth (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.3.13">Job 3:13</reference>, where the <hi type="italic">praet</hi>. more objectively expressed what would then have happened). These <hi type="italic">modi condit</hi>. are continued in <reference osisRef="Job.10.19">Job 10:19</reference> : I should have been (sc. in the womb) as though I had not been (comp. the short elliptical<note placement="foot">כלא is there = לא כאשׁר, like ללא, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.1">Isa 65:1</reference> = לא לאשׁר [<hi type="italic">vid</hi>.
